cards.title: Introduction to Lambdas in Java
cards.content:
Java 8 introduced Lambda expressions to facilitate functional programming. A lambda expression is a short block of code which takes in parameters and returns a value. Lambda expressions are similar to methods, but they do not need a name and they can be implemented right in the body of a method.

Syntax:

(parameter1, parameter2) -> { code block }

Example compared to anonymous inner class:

// Anonymous Inner Class
Runnable r1 = new Runnable() {
    @Override
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Hello World");
    }
};

// Lambda Expression
Runnable r2 = () -> System.out.println("Hello World");

cards.title: Functional Interfaces
cards.content:
A lambda expression can only be used where a functional interface is expected. A functional interface is an interface that contains exactly one abstract method. These interfaces are also known as Single Abstract Method (SAM) interfaces.

You can use the optional @FunctionalInterface annotation to have the compiler verify that the interface indeed contains only one abstract method.

@FunctionalInterface
interface MathOperation {
    int operate(int a, int b);
}

Note: Functional interfaces can have any number of default or static methods as long as they have only one abstract method.

content.text: A functional interface is an interface that contains exactly one [blank] method, which allows it to be represented by a lambda expression.

cards.title: Java's Built-in Functional Interfaces
cards.content:
The java.util.function package contains many built-in functional interfaces so you don't have to define your own. The four most commonly used are:

  • Predicate<T>: Takes an argument and returns a boolean (test method).
  • Consumer<T>: Takes an argument and returns nothing (accept method).
  • Supplier<T>: Takes no argument and returns a value (get method).
  • Function<T, R>: Takes an argument of type T and returns a result of type R (apply method).

cards.title: Method References
cards.content:
Method references are a shorthand notation of a lambda expression to call an existing method. They use the double colon operator (::).

There are four kinds of method references:

  • Reference to a static method: ContainingClass::staticMethodName
  • Reference to an instance method of a particular object: containingObject::instanceMethodName
  • Reference to an instance method of an arbitrary object of a particular type: ContainingType::methodName
  • Reference to a constructor: ClassName::new

Example: System.out::println is equivalent to x -> System.out.println(x).

cards.title: Variable Capture & Scope
cards.content:
Like anonymous inner classes, lambda expressions can capture variables from the enclosing scope. However, they can only access local variables that are final or effectively final.

An effectively final variable is one whose value is never changed after it is initialized.

int factor = 2; // effectively final
NumericOperator op = n -> n * factor; // Compile-OK

int factor2 = 3;
factor2 = 4; // modified!
NumericOperator op2 = n -> n * factor2; // Compilation Error!
